Hi Lucy —

Thanks again for taking the call yesterday. To scope dedicated capacity and give AuroraTech a tight estimate, can you fill out the quick intake below and return it with a small sample of production traces (CSV) if possible? I attached a lightweight template (workload_sample_template.csv) to make this easier.

Key items we need:
- Typical concurrency (active simultaneous sessions or requests) and expected peak concurrency
- 50/95/99th percentile prompt length (tokens) and response length (tokens) — approximate ranges are fine
- Burst windows: how often do you see 5–10x bursts (daily/hourly/weekly) and typical burst duration
- Percent of requests that are streaming vs non-streaming (estimate)
- Session affinity: are requests pinned to a session for KV cache reuse (yes/no) and typical session duration
- Any non-LLM processing on the same GPU (reranking, embeddings, vector search frequency)
- Target p95 latency SLO for user-facing requests and acceptable cost trade-offs (latency vs. $/token)
- Launch timeline and expected monthly token volume (or range)

What we’ll produce after you return this: a recommended GPU mix (SKU and counts), suggested KV cache and batching settings, and an initial queue-aware mapping that ties request priority and burst tolerance to instance pools.

If you prefer, drop a sample CSV to this thread and we’ll parse it and feed a short model of expected occupancy back to you.

Hi Neha —

Thanks — attached is a quick export from our staging traffic (auroratech_sample.csv). High-level answers below; I flagged the sample rows that correspond to our top 3 flows.

- Typical concurrency: 120 active requests on weekdays; peak concurrency historically ~900 for short windows (5–12 minutes) during product announcements.
- Prompt length: p50 45 tokens, p95 320 tokens, p99 900 tokens (we do have some very long generation jobs for summaries).
- Response length: p50 32 tokens, p95 280 tokens, p99 820 tokens.
- Bursts: 4–6 times per week (marketing pushes), usually 6–10 minutes; occasional daily bursts during regional promos.
- Streaming: ~65% of user-facing chat flows stream responses; background batch jobs are non-streaming.
- Session affinity: yes — sessions are pinned for up to 25 minutes to favor KV reuse; about 40% of traffic benefits from KV cache.
- Non-LLM load: light embedding requests for semantic search (~7% of requests) and a small internal reranker called post-rank (~3%).
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 1.2s for interactive flows; p99 <= 2.5s is preferred but we can accept higher for the longest jobs.
- Launch timeline: pilot in Q3 (target mid-August); expected monthly tokens for pilot ~750M, growth to 4–5B over 6 months.

Questions for you: what GPU mix would you recommend for the pilot vs. scale, and how do you handle short 10-minute 900-concurrency bursts without our cost exploding?

Thanks,

Neha / Marissa —

Looping in some quick observations from the sample Lucy sent and an initial mapping suggestion. Quoted Lucy below for context.

On the numbers: the p95/p99 lengths and the 900-concurrency short bursts make AuroraTech very bursty. Two levers we typically recommend: 1) a tiered pool architecture with a small hot pool (low-latency SKU) for interactive streaming flows and a larger cold pool (cost-optimized SKU) for non-streaming or long-running summarization jobs; 2) aggressive KV cache and prefix caching for sessions to reduce per-token compute on the hot pool.

Initial GPU mix (pilot):
- Hot pool: 8 x NVIDIA A100 80GB (or equivalent high-memory GPU) configured for streaming workloads and pinned session affinity. Target to serve the 120 steady concurrency with headroom for bursts via autoscaling and burst-fallback.
- Cold pool: 6 x L4 / L40-like nodes (cost-optimized) for non-streaming summarization and background reranking/embeddings.

Notes:
- With continuous batching and prefix KV reuse we can cut the hot-pool token cost by ~25–40% on flows that hit cache.
- For 10-minute 900-concurrency bursts, we recommend a burst policy that temporarily routes new sessions to ephemeral bursting capacity (short-lived instances billed at burst rates) while preserving the hot pool for priority users. This avoids overcommitting reserved fleet at steady-state.
- We’ll also recommend token-limited timeouts for extreme long jobs ( > 1200 tokens) and route those to the cold pool.

Questions for the intake follow-up:
- Can Lucy share the distribution of burst-originating requests by geographic region? If bursts are US-only we can localize bursting and keep EU capacity smaller.
- How many concurrent long-running summarization jobs (p99 range) do you see during the peak bursts? That changes cold-pool sizing.

I’ll draft a quick cost/latency tradeoff table once we have region split and long-job concurrency.

—Karthik
